Oxygen consumption was measured in quiescent, unfed adult Trinidadian guppies (Poecilia reticulata LPY) from the LP Yarra population using closed-chamber respirometry. Individuals with a mean wet body mass of 74 milligrams exhibited a resting metabolic rate of 0.0234 milligrams per hour  when acclimated to and measured at a water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This relatively modest metabolic demand is consistent with the low energetic cost of routine maintenance expected in a small-bodied poeciliid. The metabolic trials were conducted under strictly controlled conditions to minimize activity-related noise, and each fish was allowed a 30-minute equilibration period within the respirometry chamber before recordings began. The oxygen partial pressure in the chamber remained above 80% of air saturation throughout the measurement period to avoid hypoxic stress, ensuring that the recorded rate reflected basal rather than stressed metabolic conditions. All specimens were drawn from a laboratory-reared cohort maintained on a standardized high-food ration prior to the experiment.

Estimates of asymptotic body length were derived from a longitudinal growth study of first-generation offspring reared in the laboratory. The feeding regime applied to the F1 generation was designed to permit attainment of 90 percent of the maximum length achievable under ad libitum food availability. After correcting for this intentional growth restriction, the projected ultimate standard length for the LP Yarra lineage was calculated to be 3.33 centimeters [Li = 3.33 centimeters]. This asymptotic length places the LP Yarra population at the smaller end of the size spectrum among Trinidadian guppy lineages, a trait that may reflect local adaptation to the specific predation regime or resource base of the Yarra River system. Growth trajectories were fitted using repeated morphometric measurements taken every 14 days from birth until the cessation of detectable somatic growth, which typically occurred by 120 days of age.

The mean dry weight of neonates produced by females maintained on a high food ration throughout gestation was determined by drying newly parturiated offspring to constant mass at 60 °C. Recordings from a sample of 15 broods indicated a striking consistency in offspring size, with a mean dry weight at birth of 0.00102 grams  under this high-food regime. This value provides a baseline measure of the minimal material investment per offspring when maternal resources are not constrained by food limitation. In contrast, a parallel cohort of females reared on a restricted low food ration gave birth to neonates with a somewhat greater mean dry weight of 0.00110 grams . The slightly larger offspring size under low food conditions, which runs counter to a simple expectation of resource limitation, may reflect a compensatory maternal strategy that allocates a greater proportion of available resources to each individual offspring when overall fecundity is reduced, thereby enhancing offspring viability in a nutritionally challenging environment.

The interval between successive parturition events was monitored closely in individually housed females from the LP Yarra population to derive an accurate measure of gestation length and age at first birth. By calculating the mean interval across the first four parturitions for females provisioned ad libitum, the resulting estimate for the mean age at birth under high food conditions was 27.33 days [ab = 27.33 days], recorded at a stable environmental temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. This rapid developmental period is characteristic of a live-bearing poeciliid adapted to warm, productive habitats and reflects the accelerated embryonic growth permitted by a continuous supply of maternal resources. Females in the high-food treatment group consistently produced their first brood within a narrow window of this value, indicating strong canalization of the reproductive schedule when nutritional conditions are favorable and thermal conditions remain optimal for embryonic metabolism.

When the same reproductive phenology was examined in females maintained on a restricted low food diet, a notable lengthening of the developmental interval was observed. Under the identical thermal regime of 26 °C [T = 26 °C], the mean age at first parturition increased to 31.08 days [ab = 31.08 days], a delay of approximately 3.75 days relative to the high-food cohort. This extended gestation likely reflects a reduced rate of nutrient transfer from the mother to the developing embryos when the maternal energy budget is constrained, prolonging the period required for offspring to reach a viable birth size. Both the high-food and low-food estimates were derived from the same experimental design, using the mean interval between the first four parturitions as a robust proxy for the typical gestation period. The divergence between the two feeding treatments underscores the plasticity of the guppy's reproductive schedule in response to resource availability, a trait that facilitates persistence across a broad range of ecological conditions in the Yarra River system.
